lines.text: In 1731, Philadelphia had no lending library.
No fire company. No hospital. No college.
Twenty years later, it had all four, and one man had helped to start every one of them.
Benjamin Franklin was a printer by trade.
He was also a writer, a scientist, an inventor, and later, a diplomat.
A polymath: excellent across disciplines, and pointed at the public good.
His first institution solved a simple problem: in the colonies, books were rare and expensive.
So in 1731, he persuaded fifty subscribers to pay forty shillings each, and buy books together.
The Library Company of Philadelphia is still open today.
Fire was the next problem.
After warning readers that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, he organised the Union Fire Company: volunteers who pledged their own leather buckets to every blaze.
When the physician Thomas Bond wanted a hospital for the sick poor, Franklin found a clever way to pay for it.
He asked the Pennsylvania Assembly to promise two thousand pounds, but only if private donors raised two thousand of their own.
It was one of America's first matching grants.
Then came an academy, which grew into the University of Pennsylvania.
But here is the thing.
Each one had to be built from scratch: the agreements, the subscriptions, the fundraising, the books.
Franklin did it four times, alongside a printing business, an almanac, and experiments with lightning.
Today, a founder like Franklin would not have to start from zero.
A fiscal sponsor can give a new project a legal and financial home from day one, so it can accept gifts, win grants and sign contracts, while the founder gets on with the work.
That is what Mulvium is building: a home for the next Franklin.
Because the next great expansion of human creativity will come from making it easier to create institutions.
